summary: Adds an IAuditLog dependency, wraps the provider charge in CaptureAsync in a three-attempt retry loop with a catch-all handler, adds a new public RefundAsync that calls the provider and increments order.RefundedAmount, and adds a fire-and-forget RecordAudit helper.

findings.title: Charge retry has no idempotency key and can bill the customer three times
findings.detail: The charge is retried up to three times by calling `ChargeAsync(order.Id, order.Total, ct)` again, with nothing that makes a repeat call collapse into the first one. A failure after the provider has accepted the charge (read timeout, dropped connection, a 5xx returned after the money moved) is indistinguishable here from a failure before it, so the customer is billed twice or three times for `order.Total` and the method can still return false afterwards, leading the caller to report a failed capture on a paid order. A clean decline is retried too: when `result.Succeeded` is false no exception is thrown, so the loop immediately re-submits a card that was declined for a non-transient reason such as insufficient funds or a bad card.
findings.suggestion: Pass a stable idempotency key (for example the order id plus a capture attempt id) to `ChargeAsync` so a repeated call cannot create a second charge, break out of the loop when `result.Succeeded` is false, and retry only the failures the provider classifies as transient or not-yet-created.

findings.title: async void audit write is unobserved and can crash the process
findings.detail: `RecordAudit` is declared `async void`, so the call on line 25 returns at the first await and `CaptureAsync` returns true before the audit entry is written. If `_audit.WriteAsync` throws, there is no caller to observe the exception: an `async void` method rethrows on the thread pool, which is an unhandled exception and terminates the ASP.NET Core process. If it does not throw, the write is still abandoned when the request completes or the host shuts down, so captures go unrecorded exactly when the system is under stress or restarting.
findings.suggestion: Change it to `private Task RecordAuditAsync(Order order, string action)` that returns the `_audit.WriteAsync` task, and await it before returning true, wrapping it in its own try/catch and log if an audit failure must not fail the capture.

findings.title: Refund amount is sent to the provider without any validation
findings.detail: `amount` reaches this method straight from the client: `OrdersController.Refund` binds it as `[FromQuery] decimal amount` and passes it through unchecked, and nothing here validates it before `_provider.RefundAsync`. Any authenticated caller can refund more than the order total, repeat a full refund as often as they like, or pass a negative amount, which sends a negative refund to the provider and *decreases* `order.RefundedAmount`, inflating the revenue that `OrderRepository.TotalFor` computes as `Sum(Total) - Sum(RefundedAmount)`. This is money leaving the merchant account on a client-controlled value.
findings.suggestion: Before calling the provider, reject the request unless `amount > 0` and `amount <= order.Total - order.RefundedAmount`, and unless the order is in a refundable state (captured, not already fully refunded); return a typed result rather than a bare bool so the controller can distinguish invalid input from a provider failure.

findings.title: Successful refund is never persisted, so an order can be refunded repeatedly
findings.detail: `order` comes from `OrderRepository.FindAsync`, which queries with `AsNoTracking()` (src/Shop.Api/Data/OrderRepository.cs:18), and neither this method nor `OrdersController.Refund` calls `SaveChanges` (no `SaveChanges` call exists anywhere in the repository). The increment on line 41 therefore mutates a detached object that is discarded when the request ends: the provider refunds the money but the database never records it. The same order can be refunded again for the full amount with no trace, and `TotalFor` keeps reporting revenue that has already been paid back. `Status` is never moved to `OrderStatus.Refunded` either, so nothing downstream can tell a refunded order from a captured one.
findings.suggestion: Persist the refund in the same unit of work as the provider call: load the order tracked (or attach it), update `RefundedAmount` and `Status`, and save before reporting success; key the write on a refund id so a retried request cannot record the same refund twice.

findings.title: Catch-all swallows cancellation and hides every provider error
findings.detail: `catch (Exception)` has no filter and no logging. When `ct` is cancelled, `ChargeAsync` throws `OperationCanceledException`, which is caught here and treated as a transient failure: the loop sleeps and charges the card again after the caller has already gone away, and the method eventually returns false as though the payment had been declined. The same catch hides programming errors (null reference, argument validation) and discards every detail of the provider failure, since the exception object is never logged. `Task.Delay(500)` on line 31 also ignores `ct`, so a cancelled capture still takes at least a second and a half, and the delay after the third attempt is pure waiting before the loop exits.
findings.suggestion: Let `OperationCanceledException` propagate (or add `when (!ct.IsCancellationRequested)` to the catch), catch the provider's transient exception type instead of `Exception`, log the exception object, pass `ct` to `Task.Delay`, and skip the delay after the final attempt.

findings.title: RefundedAmount is increased before the provider result is checked
findings.detail: Line 41 runs unconditionally, before `result.Succeeded` is evaluated on line 42, so a refund the provider rejected still increments the order's running refunded total. Today the damage is contained only because the entity is detached and never saved; as soon as the persistence gap is closed, or any caller hands in a tracked or cached `Order` instance, every failed refund silently records a refund that never happened and permanently reduces the amount that can still be refunded.
findings.suggestion: Check `result.Succeeded` first and update `order.RefundedAmount` only on the success path.

findings.title: New async API takes no CancellationToken and hardcodes None
findings.detail: `RefundAsync` is a new public async method with no `CancellationToken` parameter, and it passes `CancellationToken.None` to the provider on line 40, so the refund call cannot be cancelled or bounded by the request lifetime and will keep running after the client disconnects or the host begins shutting down. This is inconsistent within the file: `CaptureAsync` takes a token, and `OrdersController.Refund` already has one in scope but has no way to forward it.
findings.suggestion: Add a `CancellationToken ct` parameter, pass it to `_provider.RefundAsync`, and forward the controller's token at the call site.

findings.title: Refunds write no audit entry although captures now do
findings.detail: The same change introduces an audit trail for captures (line 25), but the refund path, the one that moves money back out, writes nothing to `IAuditLog`. `CaptureAsync` also audits only the success branch, so declined and abandoned captures leave no trace either. The result is an audit log that silently covers half of the payment activity, which is worse than none because it looks complete.
findings.suggestion: Write an audit entry for refunds (order id, amount, provider result) and for capture failures through the same `IAuditLog`.

notes: For the integration pass: (1) the `PaymentService` constructor now takes an extra `IAuditLog` argument, and neither `IAuditLog` nor `IPaymentProvider` is defined anywhere in this snapshot and there is no composition root here, so the DI registration for `IAuditLog` and any other construction sites (including test doubles) need verifying. (2) `IPaymentProvider.RefundAsync(int, decimal, CancellationToken)` is used for the first time by this change; confirm the member exists on the interface and on every implementation. (3) The refund bookkeeping has no path to the database in this snapshot (`OrderRepository.FindAsync` uses `AsNoTracking()` and there is no `SaveChanges` call anywhere) - confirm against the real data layer before treating finding 4 as certain. (4) `OrdersController.Refund` binds `amount` from the query string and the controller carries only a class-level `[Authorize]` with no check that the order belongs to the caller, so the unvalidated-amount finding is reachable by any authenticated user against any order id. (5) There is no test project in this snapshot, so the retry loop and the entire refund path ship untested.

summary: Replaces the translated LINQ status filter in SearchAsync with a static string-to-OrderStatus dictionary lookup feeding an interpolated FromSqlRaw query, and adds a TotalFor helper that sums order totals minus refunded amounts.

findings.title: SearchAsync throws KeyNotFoundException for refunded, cancelled or unknown status
findings.detail: StatusMap only contains "pending" and "captured", but OrderStatus (src/Shop.Api/Models/Order.cs) also defines Refunded and Cancelled. The indexer at line 22 throws KeyNotFoundException for any other value, so a search for "refunded" - the status this PR introduces - crashes with an unhandled 500 instead of returning results. The previous implementation filtered with a Where clause and simply returned an empty list for a status it did not recognise, so this is a regression for every unmapped input, including "" and any typo. A null status additionally throws NullReferenceException on the ToLower() call.
findings.suggestion: Use Enum.TryParse<OrderStatus>(status, ignoreCase: true, out var mapped) (or TryGetValue over a map covering all four members) and return an empty list or a validation error for input that does not parse, instead of indexing the dictionary directly.

findings.title: Raw SQL compares the enum's name against a column EF maps to int by default
findings.detail: Interpolating an OrderStatus into the SQL string produces Status = 'Pending' - the enum member name. Order.Status is an OrderStatus enum, and with no HasConversion configuration EF Core persists enums as integers, so the generated predicate compares an int column to a string literal: SQL Server raises a conversion error and SQLite silently matches nothing. Going through FromSqlRaw also bypasses EF's value conversion, which the previous LINQ Where used correctly. I could not confirm the mapping because there is no ShopContext or real migration in the repository (only a stub Designer file), so this depends on how Status is configured.
findings.suggestion: Drop the raw SQL and keep the translated query: `await _db.Orders.AsNoTracking().Where(o => o.Status == mapped).ToListAsync(ct)`, which lets EF apply the column's value conversion.

findings.title: FromSqlRaw with an interpolated string bypasses parameterisation
findings.detail: FromSqlRaw($"...") concatenates the value straight into the SQL text. The value here is an enum taken from a fixed dictionary, so the caller's string never reaches the query and there is no exploitable injection today, but the pattern is one edit away from one: adding a fallback that passes the raw status through, or a new status whose name is built from input, turns this into an injection point with no compiler or analyzer warning.
findings.suggestion: Use FromSqlInterpolated, or FromSqlRaw with an explicit SqlParameter, so the value is always sent as a parameter regardless of where it comes from.

findings.title: ToLower() is culture-sensitive and can break the lookup under a Turkish locale
findings.detail: status.ToLower() uses the current culture. Under tr-TR, "PENDING".ToLower() yields "pendn" with a dotless i, so the key misses StatusMap and - because of the indexer at the same line - the request fails with KeyNotFoundException rather than degrading. Key normalisation should never depend on the server's culture.
findings.suggestion: Build StatusMap with StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase and look up status directly, or use status.ToLowerInvariant().

findings.title: TotalFor enumerates the IEnumerable three times
findings.detail: orders is walked once by Any() and twice more by the two Sum calls. When a caller passes a lazy sequence - an un-materialised IQueryable, a Where chain over the DbSet, or an iterator - the source is evaluated three times: three database round trips for one total, with the risk of summing different rows if the data changes between them. The Any() guard is also redundant, since Sum over an empty sequence already returns 0.
findings.suggestion: Compute it in one pass: `return orders.Sum(o => o.Total - o.RefundedAmount);` and drop the Any() check, or materialise with ToList() first if the guard is wanted.

notes: For the integration pass: (1) SearchAsync's contract changed from 'unknown status returns an empty list' to 'unknown status throws' - check every caller and whether the status string comes from a query parameter; there are no callers inside this repository, so a front end or another service may drive it. (2) Order.Status is an OrderStatus enum while the pre-image of this method compared it to a string, so the model type appears to have changed in this PR: verify serialization casing and any TypeScript client that sends or reads the status, plus whether a migration converts existing rows. (3) StatusMap covers 2 of the 4 OrderStatus members - if a member is ever inserted in the middle of the enum, persisted integers shift. (4) TotalFor is new public surface with no callers and no tests in the repository; PaymentService.cs:41 mutates order.RefundedAmount, so confirm which side owns the net-total calculation. (5) There is no ShopContext.cs and the only migration is a stub, so the enum-to-column mapping behind finding 2 could not be verified here.

summary: Adds a `refundOrder` client that POSTs to `/api/orders/{id}/refund?amount=`, and a `formatRefund` helper that renders the amount remaining after a refund.

findings.title: refundOrder never checks res.ok, so a failed refund resolves as success
findings.detail: Unlike captureOrder on line 10, refundOrder returns res.json() without testing res.ok. The endpoint returns Problem("Refund failed") when the provider declines (OrdersController.cs:38), which is a JSON ProblemDetails body with an error status code, so res.json() succeeds and the promise resolves with an object typed as Order whose `total` and `customerEmail` are undefined and whose `status` is the numeric HTTP status rather than the order status. Every caller sees a failed refund as a completed one, and the customer is never refunded. A non-JSON body (HTML error page, 204) instead throws an opaque SyntaxError with no mention of the status code.
findings.suggestion: Mirror captureOrder: `if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Refund failed: ${res.status}`);` before `return res.json();`.

findings.title: (remaining * 100) / 100 is a no-op, so money is rendered unrounded
findings.detail: The `* 100 / 100` idiom is the standard two-decimal rounding with the `Math.round` left out, so it cancels and returns `remaining` unchanged. Because `total` and `refunded` are floating point, a partial refund such as 49.99 - 10.10 renders as "39.89000000000001 remaining" in the UI. There is also no currency symbol or fixed 2-decimal formatting, so whole amounts render as "40 remaining".
findings.suggestion: Use a currency formatter, e.g. `return `${new Intl.NumberFormat(undefined, { style: "currency", currency: "USD" }).format(remaining)} remaining`;`, or at minimum `Math.round(remaining * 100) / 100` with `.toFixed(2)`.

notes: Contract checks for the integration pass: (1) the query-string shape matches the back end - OrdersController.Refund is `[HttpPost("{id:int}/refund")]` with `[FromQuery] decimal amount` (src/Shop.Api/Controllers/OrdersController.cs:32-33) - but the failure branch returns `Problem(...)` rather than a typed error, which is what makes the missing res.ok check above dangerous. (2) `formatRefund` is exported but has no callers anywhere in the repository, so the rounding defect is latent rather than currently visible. (3) The only caller of `refundOrder` is web/src/pages/OrderPage.tsx:12, which calls it inside an onClick without awaiting the promise, without a catch and without disabling the button; combined with a refund endpoint that has no idempotency key, repeated clicks can issue multiple refunds and no error can ever reach the user. (4) `Order.total` is `number` here while the back-end model uses `decimal` (src/Shop.Api/Models/Order.cs), so all money math in this file is floating point.

summary: Replaces the string `Status` property on the `Order` entity with a new `OrderStatus` enum (Pending/Captured/Refunded/Cancelled) and adds a `RefundedAmount` decimal property.

findings.title: Status becomes an int column and RefundedAmount is new, with no migration
findings.detail: Status previously mapped to a string column: the base OrderRepository filtered with `o.Status == status` translated to SQL, and the head version still compares against the enum name as a SQL string literal ('Captured'). Under EF Core's default enum mapping the property now maps to an int column, and RefundedAmount adds a column that does not exist at all. Against an already-deployed database every read of Orders fails to materialize (invalid column / conversion error) rather than degrading gracefully. The only file touched under Migrations/ in this PR bumps a version constant and describes no schema change, so nothing converts the existing 'Pending'/'Captured' values or backfills the new column.
findings.suggestion: Either keep the column shape by configuring `builder.Entity<Order>().Property(o => o.Status).HasConversion<string>()` in ShopContext, or add a migration that converts Status to int with a backfill of the existing text values; in both cases add a migration for RefundedAmount with a default of 0 for existing rows.

findings.title: Enum Status changes the JSON response from a string to a number
findings.detail: System.Text.Json serializes enums as numbers unless JsonStringEnumConverter is registered, and OrdersController returns the Order entity directly from Capture and Refund, so a response field that carried "Pending" now carries 0. web/src/api/orders.ts is modified in this PR but still declares `status: string`, and the `canRefund` check added to web/src/pages/OrderPage.tsx in this PR compares `order.status === "captured"`, which can never be true: the Refund button never renders and the status is rendered as a bare digit. Registering the string converter alone does not fix it either, since the default serialized name is "Captured", not "captured".
findings.suggestion: Register `JsonStringEnumConverter` (with a camelCase naming policy if the client expects lowercase names) and change the TypeScript `Order.status` to the matching string union, or expose the status as a string on a DTO instead of returning the entity's enum.

findings.title: OrderStatus members have implicit values that now define stored data
findings.detail: If Status ends up persisted with EF's default int mapping, the declaration order of these four members silently becomes the on-disk contract for 0-3, with nothing in the code saying so. Inserting a status later (for example PartiallyRefunded after Captured) renumbers every existing row's meaning without any compiler or migration signal.
findings.suggestion: Assign explicit values (`Pending = 0, Captured = 1, Refunded = 2, Cancelled = 3`), or persist the enum as a string so member order carries no meaning.

notes: ShopContext is not present in the reviewed tree and there is no Program.cs/appsettings here, so the actual EF mapping for Status (a HasConversion<string>() would change finding 1) and any JsonStringEnumConverter registration (finding 2) could not be confirmed - the integration pass should verify both. Other consumers of the changed Status type: src/Shop.Api/Data/OrderRepository.cs now builds `FromSqlRaw($"SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE Status = '{mapped}'")` from the enum's name, web/src/api/orders.ts still types status as string, and web/src/pages/OrderPage.tsx compares it to the literal "captured". Separately, nothing in the visible code ever assigns Captured, Refunded or Cancelled; RefundedAmount is only incremented in PaymentService.RefundAsync with no check against Total and no status transition, so an order can be fully refunded while Status is still Pending and can be refunded repeatedly past its total.

summary: Adds a POST api/orders/{id}/refund endpoint that loads the order by id and calls PaymentService.RefundAsync with an amount taken from the query string, returning the order on success. Also adds a using for Shop.Api.Models.

findings.title: Refund amount from the query string is never validated or capped
findings.detail: `amount` is bound straight from the query string and handed to the provider with no bounds check, and PaymentService.RefundAsync (src/Shop.Api/Services/PaymentService.cs:38-43) does not validate it either. POST /api/orders/5/refund?amount=999999 refunds far more than the order total; ?amount=-50 sends a negative refund to the provider and decrements order.RefundedAmount, moving the ledger backwards; ?amount=0 calls the provider and returns 200 for a no-op. Nothing compares the request against order.Total - order.RefundedAmount, and nothing checks that the order was ever captured (order.Status is still Pending for an uncaptured order), so a pending order can be refunded.
findings.suggestion: Reject amount <= 0 with BadRequest, require order.Status == OrderStatus.Captured, and cap the refund at order.Total - order.RefundedAmount before calling _payments.RefundAsync.

findings.title: New refund endpoint has no ownership or role check on the order
findings.detail: The class-level [Authorize] at line 11 carries no policy or role, so it only proves the caller is signed in, and OrderRepository.FindAsync (src/Shop.Api/Data/OrderRepository.cs:17-18) filters by id alone. Any authenticated user can therefore enumerate integer ids and trigger refunds against orders that belong to other customers, and the response body at line 38 returns that order including CustomerEmail. Refunds move money out, so this is a materially bigger exposure than the pre-existing capture endpoint.
findings.suggestion: Require an admin/refund policy on this action, or load the order scoped to the caller (for example FindForUserAsync(id, User, ct)) and return NotFound when it is not theirs.

findings.title: Refund is never persisted, so repeat calls refund from a zero base
findings.detail: FindAsync returns an AsNoTracking() entity (src/Shop.Api/Data/OrderRepository.cs:18) and PaymentService.RefundAsync mutates order.RefundedAmount on that detached instance (src/Shop.Api/Services/PaymentService.cs:41). There is no SaveChanges/SaveChangesAsync call anywhere in the repository, and order.Status is never moved to OrderStatus.Refunded. The response at line 38 reports the new RefundedAmount, so the client believes the refund was recorded, while the database still shows 0 refunded; the next request re-reads a stale 0, meaning the same order can be refunded repeatedly with no cumulative cap, and OrderRepository.TotalFor keeps returning pre-refund revenue.
findings.suggestion: Load the order tracked for this path, update RefundedAmount and Status after the provider confirms, and persist with SaveChangesAsync(ct) inside the same unit of work before returning.

findings.title: CancellationToken is accepted but not passed to the refund call
findings.detail: The action takes `ct` and uses it for the lookup at line 35, but _payments.RefundAsync(order, amount) takes no token, and PaymentService hard-codes CancellationToken.None for the provider call (src/Shop.Api/Services/PaymentService.cs:40). The sibling capture path at line 28 does pass `ct`, so this is copy-paste drift: the outbound provider request has no cancellation or timeout linkage to the request, and the parameter's presence in the signature is misleading.
findings.suggestion: Add a CancellationToken parameter to PaymentService.RefundAsync and forward `ct` to it, matching CaptureAsync.

findings.title: Declined refund returns HTTP 500 instead of a client-facing error
findings.detail: Problem("Refund failed") with no status produces 500 Internal Server Error, but a provider decline is an expected business outcome, not a server fault. It pollutes error-rate alerting, and the browser client (web/src/api/orders.ts refundOrder) never checks res.ok, so it parses the ProblemDetails body as an Order and the UI shows a refund that did not happen. The capture path at line 29 has the same shape, so fixing both keeps them consistent.
findings.suggestion: Return a 4xx with the reason, for example Problem(detail: "Refund declined by provider", statusCode: StatusCodes.Status409Conflict), and have the TypeScript client check res.ok.

notes: For the integration pass: (1) new route POST /api/orders/{id}/refund?amount= is consumed by refundOrder in web/src/api/orders.ts, which ignores res.ok and whose Order interface has no refundedAmount field, so the value this endpoint returns is outside the TS contract; (2) PaymentService.RefundAsync(Order, decimal) is new public surface without a CancellationToken parameter and it mutates the passed entity; (3) OrderRepository.FindAsync is AsNoTracking() and the repository contains no SaveChanges/SaveChangesAsync anywhere, so confirm how any order state is meant to be persisted; (4) no test project exists in the repository, so the new endpoint ships without tests; (5) no Program.cs is present in the change set, so a global authorization fallback policy could not be checked for the [Authorize] finding.

summary: Adds a Refund button to OrderSummary that renders only when order.status is "captured" and calls the new refundOrder(order.id, order.total) API helper on click.

findings.title: Refund button fires and forgets, so repeat clicks refund the order twice
findings.detail: The onClick handler calls refundOrder(order.id, order.total) and throws the promise away. Nothing tracks the in-flight request: the button is never disabled, and `order` is a prop, so `canRefund` and the status span at line 9 keep their old values until the parent happens to refetch. A user who clicks twice - or clicks again because the first click produced no visible feedback - posts /api/orders/{id}/refund a second time, and PaymentService.RefundAsync accumulates with `order.RefundedAmount += amount` and no idempotency key, so the customer is refunded the full total twice. The discarded promise also means a rejected fetch surfaces only as an unhandled rejection in the console, with the UI still showing a clickable Refund button.
findings.suggestion: Give the component local state for the request (e.g. `const [refunding, setRefunding] = useState(false)`), set it before the call and disable the button while it is true, and make the handler async: await refundOrder, hand the returned Order back to the parent so the status re-renders, and catch failures into a visible error.

findings.title: canRefund compares status to "captured", which the API likely never returns
findings.detail: The front-end Order type declares `status: string`, but the API returns Shop.Api.Models.Order whose Status is the OrderStatus enum. I found no JsonStringEnumConverter or JsonSerializerOptions configuration anywhere under src/, so System.Text.Json serializes Status as a number (1), and even with that converter registered the value would be "Captured", not "captured". In either case canRefund is always false and the Refund button never renders, so the feature ships dead. Because status is a bare `string`, nothing in the build catches the mismatch.
findings.suggestion: Confirm what the API actually emits for Status, then mirror it as a union on the Order interface (e.g. `status: "Pending" | "Captured" | "Refunded" | "Cancelled"`) so this comparison is type-checked instead of silently false.

notes: For the integration pass: (1) verify the OrderStatus serialization contract between src/Shop.Api/Models/Order.cs and web/src/api/orders.ts - no serializer configuration was visible in the repository, and OrderRepository.cs maps the lowercase string "captured" to OrderStatus.Captured, which suggests two different status vocabularies are in play; (2) the backend Order has RefundedAmount but the TypeScript Order interface does not, so this component always sends the full order.total and cannot account for a prior partial refund - the backend Refund endpoint appears to accept that without checking the remaining balance; (3) refundOrder in web/src/api/orders.ts does not check res.ok (unlike captureOrder), so even an awaited call here would treat a Problem() response as success.
